title: de Broglie Waves
notes: Reading λ = h/p the other way, a measured wavelength gives the momentum p = h/λ. Electron diffraction fringes are therefore a momentum measurement.
An electron microscope forms an image with electrons rather than light. The shorter wavelength, at tens of kilovolts, gives a finer limit of resolution than a light microscope.

The wave packet that represents a localised particle is a spread of wavelengths. A narrow packet, a well known position, needs a wide spread of momenta. That is the idea behind the uncertainty principle.
A photon already had E = h f and p = E/c, which is the same λ = h/p. De Broglie's step was to give massive particles the relation that light already satisfied.
At higher voltage the electron is faster, the wavelength is shorter, and the non-relativistic √V formula starts to fail. Exam calculations at 100 to 200 V are still in the safe range.
The particle is not smeared into a wave in the detector. Many electrons build the diffraction pattern one impact at a time. Each impact is local. The pattern is the wave.
confusion: ❌ Wavelength is proportional to energy ✅ Wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum (λ = h/p), not energy directly.
❌ de Broglie waves apply only to charged particles ✅ Applicable to all matter, including neutral particles like neutrons, if they have momentum.
❌ Wave nature is observed in macroscopic objects ✅ Due to the extremely small value of Planck's constant (h), the wavelength of macroscopic objects is negligible and undetectable.
The microscope's advantage is the short wavelength, not a brighter lamp.
Uncertainty is a wave-packet fact, not a clumsy instrument.
Do not use the electron √V formula for a photon.
A single electron does not draw the whole fringe pattern.

exercises.question: An electron is accelerated through 150 V. Find its wavelength in angstroms with λ ≈ 12.25 / √V, and explain the slight change of the constant from 12.27.
steps: The constant 12.25 or 12.27 depends on the rounding of h, m and e.
Either constant is acceptable if you say which one you used.
150 V still gives a wavelength of atomic size, and the electron is not near the speed of light.
